title: Missile Defense: Knowledge-Based Process Would Benefit Airborne Laser Decision-Making
abstract: This document discusses the Missile Defense Agency's strategy for acquiring ballistic missile defense systems. GAO issued a report on July 12, 2002, that examined whether the Missile Defense Agency's new strategy for developing the Airborne Laser includes practices that are characteristic of successful developmental programs. Our observations today will reflect the knowledge that we gained from that work. If the Department of Defense is successful in its efforts to develop and field the Airborne Laser, it could be an important system because it would give the United States some capability to destroy enemy missiles over the enemy's own territory. Enemy states that could launch ballistic missiles with chemical or biological warheads toward the United States, its deployed troops, or allies could be deterred from doing so if that enemy knew that the chemical and biological agents might fall back to earth over its own territory.

title: Teacher-Student Representational Alignment for Reinforcement Learning-Driven Imitation Learning
abstract: Imitation learning (IL) from a state-based reinforcement learning (RL) policy is a common approach to overcome the curse of dimensionality in complex and high-dimensional observation spaces prevalent in robotics. This paper addresses the irreducible imitation gap that emerges when teacher and student are learned in isolation, and the teacher policy has the liberty to rely on privileged state information that the student cannot infer from its observations. Instead of improving poor student performance with RL finetuning after IL, which often requires a whole new training setup, we propose a novel algorithm which learns a shared embedding space that hides agent-specific observations and thus trains imitable teacher policies by construction. We train the shared embedding space with self-supervised contrastive learning in parallel to the teacher policy and prevent it from extracting private information by limiting its gradients from updating the encoder networks. We perform evaluations on several example domains and compare to state-of-the-art baselines showing that our algorithm enables higher student performance with substantially reduced imitation gap.

title: Features and Operation of an Autonomous Agent for Cyber Defense
abstract: An ever increasing number of battlefield devices that are capable of collecting, processing, storing, and communicating information are rapidly becoming interconnected. The staggering number of connected devices on the battlefield greatly increases the possibility that an adversary could find ways to exploit hardware or software vulnerabilities, degrading or denying Warfighters the assured and secure use of those devices. Autonomous software agents will become necessities to manage, defend, and react to cyber threats in the future battlespace. The number of connected devices increases disproportionately to the number of cyber experts that could be available within an operational environment. In this paper, an autonomous agent capability and a scenario of how it could operate are proposed. The goal of developing such capability is to increase the security posture of the Internet of Battlefield Things and meet the challenges of an increasingly complex battlefield. This paper describes an illustrative scenario in a notional use case and discusses the challenges associated with such autonomous agents. We conclude by offering ideas for potential research into developing autonomous agents suitable for cyber defense in a battlefield environment.

title: WaterCopilot: An AI-Driven Virtual Assistant for Water Management
abstract: Sustainable water resource management in transboundary river basins is challenged by fragmented data, limited real-time access, and the complexity of integrating diverse information sources. This paper presents WaterCopilot-an AI-driven virtual assistant developed through collaboration between the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and Microsoft Research for the Limpopo River Basin (LRB) to bridge these gaps through a unified, interactive platform. Built on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and tool-calling architectures, WaterCopilot integrates static policy documents and real-time hydrological data via two custom plugins: the iwmi-doc-plugin, which enables semantic search over indexed documents using Azure AI Search, and the iwmi-api-plugin, which queries live databases to deliver dynamic insights such as environmental-flow alerts, rainfall trends, reservoir levels, water accounting, and irrigation data. The system features guided multilingual interactions (English, Portuguese, French), transparent source referencing, automated calculations, and visualization capabilities. Evaluated using the RAGAS framework, WaterCopilot achieves an overall score of 0.8043, with high answer relevancy (0.8571) and context precision (0.8009). Key innovations include automated threshold-based alerts, integration with the LRB Digital Twin, and a scalable deployment pipeline hosted on AWS. While limitations in processing non-English technical documents and API latency remain, WaterCopilot establishes a replicable AI-augmented framework for enhancing water governance in data-scarce, transboundary contexts. The study demonstrates the potential of this AI assistant to support informed, timely decision-making and strengthen water security in complex river basins.

title: Imagining Possibility within Policy: LeAnne Howe's Shell Shaker and Louis Owens's Bone Game
abstract: In this essay, Gina Caison argues that literature by southeastern Native writers can offer new ways to imagine repatriation and return that help scholars think about the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) from a more holistic viewpoint, one that privileges the category of the agentic human dead over the category of the disinterred and often disembodied remains. Within this framework, this article examines two Choctaw novels set shortly after the 1990 passage of the NAGPRA: LeAnne Howe's Shell Shaker (2001) and Louis Owens's Bone Game (1994). Caison considers these two texts within the early nineties political moment in order to understand how they contribute to dialogue regarding the return of human remains following the passage of one of the most important pieces of legislation to affect Native communities' relationship to their pasts. Howe's and Owens's novels offer embodiment to Native human remains, and in doing so, they contribute to an understanding of NAGPRA as a legislation of homecoming with all the attenuating pain such a process can entail. Ultimately, she argues that these literary narratives allow us to retheorize and develop an Indigenous reading of the law that sees past the matter of the dead object into the life of agentic continuance.

title: Can LLMs Take the Pulse of the Economy? A Real-Time Evaluation of LLM Nowcasts on Macroeconomic Indicators
abstract: Nowcasting headline macroeconomic indicators, i.e., estimating an indicator's value for the current reference period before its official release, is critical for monetary policy and financial markets, and central banks devote dedicated teams of expert economists to producing such estimates. Large language model (LLM) agents are a promising candidate for this task, combining broad world knowledge with real-time web search and supporting queries at higher frequency than institutional nowcasts. Evaluating their nowcasting capability is, however, challenging: headline indicators such as GDP and CPI are widely reported and likely memorized during pretraining, so any evaluation on historical releases is vulnerable to data contamination. To address this, we introduce LiveMacroEval, a live, contamination-resistant benchmark in which LLM agents produce hourly nowcasts for sixteen major U.S. macroeconomic indicators over a pre-release window closing at each official release. Nowcast quality is assessed through a LiveMacro Score against announcement-window equity returns and a LiveBetting Score from simulated Polymarket-style trading, with Federal Reserve regional-bank nowcasts, the Bloomberg ECOS professional consensus, and an auto-ARIMA baseline as comparators. Over six months with four state-of-the-art LLM agents configured with web search, aggregate nowcast accuracy is broadly comparable to the institutional and professional benchmarks, with performance varying widely across individual indicators. This highlights LLM agents' potential as real-time estimators of macroeconomic conditions.

title: Active Neural Localization
abstract: Localization is the problem of estimating the location of an autonomous agent from an observation and a map of the environment. Traditional methods of localization, which filter the belief based on the observations, are sub-optimal in the number of steps required, as they do not decide the actions taken by the agent. We propose "Active Neural Localizer", a fully differentiable neural network that learns to localize accurately and efficiently. The proposed model incorporates ideas of traditional filtering-based localization methods, by using a structured belief of the state with multiplicative interactions to propagate belief, and combines it with a policy model to localize accurately while minimizing the number of steps required for localization. Active Neural Localizer is trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning. We use a variety of simulation environments for our experiments which include random 2D mazes, random mazes in the Doom game engine and a photo-realistic environment in the Unreal game engine. The results on the 2D environments show the effectiveness of the learned policy in an idealistic setting while results on the 3D environments demonstrate the model's capability of learning the policy and perceptual model jointly from raw-pixel based RGB observations. We also show that a model trained on random textures in the Doom environment generalizes well to a photo-realistic office space environment in the Unreal engine.

title: Professionalism
abstract: The upsurge of interest in medical professionalism is evidenced by the increased volume of books and journal articles on the topic over the past decade or so. Several factors have contributed to this, including increasing commercialization and commoditization of medicine, well publicized examples of conflict of interest, and reports of poor and uneven quality and safety combined with escalating costs. While patients continue to place trust in their doctors, the public perception of the profession has suffered. Criticism has been leveled that self-interest trumps that of society and some view the profession as being unwilling or incapable of dealing with important health care issues. This is not good for patients, doctors, or society for it undermines the compact that has existed between them. Medical socialites, educational accrediting bodies and others have responded by embarking on a journey aimed at reversing the trend. The Charter on Professionalism, a project of the ABIM Foundation, ACP–ASIM Foundation, and European Federation of Internal Medicine, was published in 2002.1 The Charter identified three principles and ten commitments of professionalism and was promptly endorsed by over ninety learned medical organizational societies worldwide. The Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) and the American Board of Medical Specialties’ (ABMS) joint initiative identifies professionalism as one of six competencies that must be satisfied for specialty board eligibility.2 Several useful working definitions have been proposed. Most share the tenet that professional values and behavior and the attributes that underpin them must inform not only the individual doctor–patient relationship but also the broader role of medicine. The definition that appeared in the Royal College of Physicians of London (2005) report, “Doctors in Society,” posited that “Professionalism signifies a set of values, behaviors and relationships that underpins the trust the public has in doctors”.2,3 Core professionalism attributes include altruism, excellence, accountability and humanism. To these may be added self-reflection, skillful communication, dutifulness and teamwork. The hallmarks of a profession include competence in a specialized body of knowledge, acknowledgment of specific duties and responsibilities and the autonomy to train, admit, monitor and discipline its members, a privilege granted through licensure. The goals of professionalism training and education include not only imparting its duties and responsibilities but also to be transformative and result in “the development of the professional self in students; the internalization of the values and virtues of medicine as a calling”.3,4 Increasingly, medical schools admission committees assess applicants’ altruistic and empathetic potential through approaches that include the “multi mini interview” process. Professionalism training and assessment incorporates a number of validated approaches.4–6 These occur both within the formal curriculum (what is taught in lectures and seminars) and in the informal curriculum (what is observed by learners as they navigate medical school and residency training). The latter has a profound and long lasting influence as learners observe the attitudes and behavior of faculty, mentors and others more senior to them. The implications are far reaching as learners commonly model, internalize and subsequently express similar attitudes. The hidden curriculum refers to what learners interpret from the rules, regulations and priorities that govern the educational milieu.7 The null curriculum refers to missed opportunities to impart important messages to learners during training. The scope of professional duties has expanded in concert with the growth of medical knowledge and complexity. Professional commitments that apply to patients are accompanied by those towards learners, students, colleagues, non-physician members of the health care team, affiliated medical institutions, specialty societies and ultimately to society. Duties to patients are central to the nature and conduct of the doctor–patient relationship as reflected in and dominated by placing the welfare of patients first and require the willingness and skill to understand and satisfy their genuine needs. Professional responsibilities also inform health care quality, safety, service and affordability.8 The mantra “primum non nocere” reminds us of the duty to protect the safety of patients and shield them from harm. This requires vigilance, excellence and accountability, a willingness to seek advice from colleagues, pursuit of knowledge and familiarity with appropriately vetted and accepted guidelines and treatment recommendations. There is the duty to be a reliable and trusted member of the health care team as the growth of medical information outstrips the ability of individual doctors to learn, retain and practice it. As medical complexity rapidly increases, so does the need for teamwork skills in order that patients can benefit from integrated expertise. Superior communication is important to good patient outcomes, to quality and safety and the overall team effectiveness of care. Flawed communication has been cited as the singe most common contributor to sentinel events in hospitals. Healthcare costs in America (and elsewhere) are rapidly becoming unsustainable and this carries with it clear implications not only for policy makers and the public but also the medical profession. The third fundamental principle of the Charter on Professionalism calls on physicians to “promote social justice in the healthcare system including the fair distribution of health care resources.” This clearly resonates currently as health care and its funding are undergoing a transformation both in the United States and several other countries. Physicians and their professional societies have a clear and present responsibility to serve as trusted agents and advocates for their individual patients and for the overall health of the public. There are several ways in which the profession can be influential including a willingness to address the huge regional variations in health care costs unaccompanied by improvements in quality and outcome and in some cases a measurable decrement.5,9 The most important contributor to differences across locations and across regions lies in discrepancies in the number and frequency of tests and procedures undertaken to evaluate similar medical conditions. This has focused greater attention on the fee for service reimbursement system, in which volume is financially rewarded rather than quality and value and calls into question the trustworthiness of the profession. Here, therefore, is an opportunity for physicians to reassert their professionalism and their compact with society by addressing changes in individual behavior and collectively by exerting influence through their specialty and professional societies.6,10 In order to regain trust and ultimately to remain relevant, the profession must strive to reassert the values and beliefs that for many prompted the great majority of its members to enter medical school in the first place. This requires an unwavering commitment to placing the needs of the patient first and a principled approach, nimble and effective action in addressing issues of health care quality, safety, affordability and value. This will require some modification of individual physician behavior combined with the collective influence of professional societies and associations. Long-term success requires a restructuring of medical education and the goals and priorities of continuous professional development. What needs to be emphasized is not only the acquisition of knowledge but educational experiences that serve to inculcate and nurture teamwork, communication skills and a more profound understanding and appreciation of professional values and virtue. Such an outcome would help regain public trust and contribute to the restoration of the autonomy previously enjoyed by the profession; one that sadly has been replaced by an increasingly burdensome culture of compliance. Success will do much to restore the joy and fulfillment that comes from being a doctor and serves to nurture and sustain them as they strive to meet their heavy responsibilities as healers.

title: A Review of “Do Anything Now” Jailbreak Attacks in Large Language Models: Potential Risks, Impacts, and Defense Strategies
abstract: This review investigated the “Do Anything Now” (DAN) jailbreak phenomenon in Large Language Models (LLMs), which bypassed safety mechanisms through adversarial prompting, prompt injection, and persona manipulation. We analyzed its multifaceted risks: (1) technical and behavioral harms, such as the facilitation of illicit content and malicious code; (2) psychological and social manipulation, including emotional dependency and deceptive interactions; and (3) online abuse, misinformation, and the cross-model portability of jailbreaks. To mitigate these threats, we synthesized defense strategies at three levels: (1) prompt-level defenses such as input filtering, prompt rewriting, and output moderation that aimed to intercept jailbreak attempts without altering model weights; (2) model-level defenses including safety fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and internal signal monitoring to build intrinsic resistance to adversarial prompts; and (3) external and composite strategies such as multi-agent safety architectures, moving-target defenses, and continuous evaluation pipelines to provide layered protection and adaptability. We also note the ethics challenge raised by jailbreak research and evaluation practices, and outline open questions around responsibility, consent, and dual-use risk. We concluded that a defense-in-depth approach, supported by benchmark-driven evaluation and collaborative oversight, was essential for LLMs’ robust and trustworthy deployment.

title: Trackable Skill Library Lifecycle Management for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Skill-augmented agentic RL has emerged as an effective approach to improving LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. Despite this progress, individual skills may follow distinct trajectories as the policy evolves, with some becoming redundant after the model internalizes their capabilities, others remaining valuable as external scaffolding, and still others turning harmful. However, existing skill library systems fail to identify each skill's true contribution due to free-riding among co-retrieved skills, difficulty confounding across tasks, and the absence of skill-specific counterfactual evidence, which prevents reliable skill lifecycle management. We propose TrackRL, an agentic RL framework where skill tracking drives skill library full lifecycle management. Specifically, within each GRPO group, we turn grouped sampling into online randomized controlled experiments. Independent random injection and within-group contrasts on the same task isolate each skill's true contribution, and reliability-weighted aggregation accumulates evidence across groups. As evidence accumulates, we continuously track skill utility, which measures the skill's causal contribution as external scaffolding, and model mastery, which reflects how far the corresponding capability has been internalized. Along this line, we formulate skill lifecycle management as an evidence-gated state-transition process that governs each skill from generation and admission through protected incubation to retention, retirement, or removal, while a soft capacity bound controls library growth. Experiments show that TrackRL outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines in both library-assisted and skill-free evaluation, with further analyses revealing how skill value shifts during policy learning and how evidence-driven state transitions shape skill library evolution. Our code is available at https://github.com/xizhu1022/TrackRL.

title: Dual Self-Awareness Value Decomposition Framework without Individual Global Max for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Value decomposition methods have gained popularity in the field of cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. However, almost all existing methods follow the principle of Individual Global Max (IGM) or its variants, which limits their problem-solving capabilities. To address this, we propose a dual self-awareness value decomposition framework, inspired by the notion of dual self-awareness in psychology, that entirely rejects the IGM premise. Each agent consists of an ego policy for action selection and an alter ego value function to solve the credit assignment problem. The value function factorization can ignore the IGM assumption by utilizing an explicit search procedure. On the basis of the above, we also suggest a novel anti-ego exploration mechanism to avoid the algorithm becoming stuck in a local optimum. As the first fully IGM-free value decomposition method, our proposed framework achieves desirable performance in various cooperative tasks.

title: Comparative Analysis of Transformer Models for Prompt Injection Detection in Autonomous Large Language Model Agents
abstract: Prompt injection attacks pose a significant security challenge for large language model systems, particularly autonomous large language model-based agents that may interact with external tools, application programming interfaces, and data sources.This study presents a comparative evaluation of five pre-trained transformer models, namely BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, DistilBERT, and ALBERT, fine-tuned for binary prompt injection classification.A balanced dataset of 4,224 samples was compiled from 10 publicly accessible corpora containing benign and injection prompts and divided into training (2,956), validation (634), and test (634) sets.The models were trained in the Kaggle environment using an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, the AdamW optimizer, and a linear warm-up scheduling strategy.On the held-out test set, RoBERTa achieved the highest classification performance, with 97.48% accuracy, 97.52% macro-precision, 97.48% macro-recall, 97.48% macro-F1-score, and 99.64% area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.DistilBERT achieved the highest reported throughput of 819.13 samples/s and the lowest per-sample latency of 1.22 ms.Statistical analysis using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and SHapley Additive exPlanations-based interpretability analysis were also conducted to examine model differences and influential linguistic features.The findings demonstrate that fine-tuned transformer classifiers can achieve strong performance on the evaluated benchmark dataset while exhibiting different accuracyefficiency characteristics.However, the results should be interpreted within the scope of the evaluated data distribution, as the study does not include independent external datasets or adaptive adversarial attacks.These limitations indicate that further validation is required to establish generalizability and robustness in real-world prompt-injection defense scenarios.

title: Abstraction Liquidity Theory
abstract: Abstraction Liquidity Theory (ALT) develops a formal framework for determining when local problem-solving traces become reusable abstraction assets that reduce downstream search, evaluation, and certification costs. The paper treats abstractions as operational tokens rather than informal artifacts, and evaluates them through declared receivers, opportunity measures, baselines, lifecycle costs, telemetry, evidence validity, transport scope, authority envelopes, hazard constraints, and runtime certificate packets. The manuscript introduces an actor-neutral certification kernel for AI agents and other computational actors. It specifies machine-readable packet schemas, dual exploration and settlement ledgers, finite-sample lower and upper bounds, causal and calibrated-proxy value estimands, mission-validity certificates, adversarial-token rejection, root/finality checks, baseline refresh, deprecation, resurrection, rollback, and kernel-update bridges. The goal is to make abstraction evaluation executable: an agent should be able to parse a packet, verify evidence, admit or reject a token, suspend stale claims, deprecate negative-liquidity tokens, and preserve raw net safe capital under fail-closed rules. The paper further defines Target-valid ALT-CARA, a criterion for certified ASI realization acceleration. Rather than claiming unconstrained ASI achievement, ALT-CARA formalizes time-to-target acceleration relative to a resource-matched baseline upper envelope, under declared capability bases, target-validity certificates, raw net solvency, viability conditions, hazard and authority constraints, transport validity, finality, and causal reproduction evidence. The framework connects AI evaluation, causal inference, runtime verification, risk control, skill reuse, safe exploration, and distributed certification into a single theory of mission-valid safe abstraction capital.

title: Automating the seismic-resilient design of fiber-reinforced concrete using a physics-informed multi-agent system
abstract: The design of dynamically resilient concrete materials remains a complex, fragmented process that depends on iterative modelling, expert judgment, and poorly integrated workflows spanning structural analysis, material formulation, and seismic performance evaluation. To address this challenge, we develop an autonomous multi-agent system (MAS) that optimizes the life cycle design of fiber-reinforced concrete (FRC) for earthquake resilience. The system focuses on shear walls, beams, and columns that constitute the seismic load bearing envelope of multi-storey buildings. Rather than functioning as a general-purpose structural tool, the MAS is designed to intelligently generate FRC specifications, tailoring fiber type, geometry, and reinforcement ratios according to seismic inputs and project constraints that are automatically parsed by the system. The framework integrates agentic artificial intelligence (AgenAI) via an Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol with physical artificial intelligence (PhysAI) implemented through physics informed stochastic models for micromechanical prediction and energy dissipation damage analysis. A modified maximum entropy principle models fiber matrix interactions under heterogeneous uncertainty, enabling unbiased optimization of energy dissipative properties. In parallel, a CNN based computer vision pipeline employing a 3D U-Net architecture performs accurate segmentation and interpretation of micro-CT data. The architecture comprises five specialized AI agents built on Qwen-30B-A3B and Phi-4-14B large language models (LLMs), with context grounding provided by agentic retrieval augmented generation (ARAG) for domain specific decision making. Experimental validation shows that the system reduces human intensive design cycles by 75% relative to conventional finite element analysis workflows. It achieves 89.2% reasoning adherence, a mean predictive bias below 4% compared with stochastic simulations, and a failure state classification F1 score of 0.98. These results bridge micromechanical realism and automated, code compliant seismic design.

title: Privilege-Differential Drift: Measuring Mandate Inflation in Hierarchical LLM Agent Systems — A Pre-Registration
abstract: This pre-registration states a hypothesis in the intersection of two lines of work on LLM agent security: that the size of the privilege gap between the agent writing shared state and the agent reading it is itself a predictor of policy violation, under the constraint that every individual write is benign in isolation and no adversary is present at any point in the chain. The document defines a primary metric — the Mandate Inflation Rate (MIR) — specifies a three-level experimental protocol across five data categories, and pre-commits to the conditions under which the hypothesis is to be considered refuted. A null result will be published. Prior work on adversarial memory poisoning, endogenous safety drift, and self-propagating misalignment is cited and explicitly excluded from the novelty claim. This version contains no results. Version 0.2 registers the design: the frozen task set with machine-readable mandates, the tool allowlists defining the three authority levels and the privilege gaps they induce, and the power analysis — each published as executable code under test. It also records four revisions to v0.1, all made before any data collection: the sample size is resized against H2 rather than H1 and allows for the discard rate the falsification criteria permit; the control-category criterion is restated as an equivalence test, since a failure to reject is not evidence of no conditioning; model family becomes a fixed rather than a random effect; and the two comparisons in the primary hypothesis are distinguished by what each can establish. At that version the harness was still withheld. Version 0.3 adds the experimental harness: a deterministic policy gate and an append-only, hash-chained event journal, both published as code under test. Four properties of the gate determine what the primary metric counts, and the protocol now records them rather than leaving them to the implementation. The gate establishes a candidate rather than a confirmed inflation event, because the two remaining conditions — that the state rather than the task is causal, and that every entry implicated is benign in isolation — are decided by the ablation procedure and the benignness review, not at the tool boundary. An attempt by the writing agent outside its own brief feeds the discard rate rather than the numerator of the metric, since the hypothesis concerns the consuming agent and a writer stepping outside its brief puts the premise of that run in doubt. Blocked invocations are logged rather than executed, because executing a denied action would change the state the remainder of the run reads from and the ablation re-run would no longer compare like with like. An attempt outside the agent’s own capability set is counted as an escalation attempt rather than an inflation event, which the definition excludes by requiring the action to be one the agent was already permitted. The threats to validity now also record the granularity at which the gate decides: it matches on tool names, not on the arguments a tool is called with. A consumer using a permitted tool against a resource the mandate did not contemplate will pass. The resulting bias runs in one direction only — towards missing events, never towards inventing them — so a measured MIR is a lower bound on the quantity the study defines. The background section additionally distinguishes a near neighbour that removes both the adversary and the capability confound, but does so at a single decision point with a single agent, where there is no writer, no shared state, and no authority differential. This version also corrects two figures that still described the v0.1 sample size after the design was resized in v0.2. The registered design is unchanged at 135 runs per cell and 6,075 total. A test now parses the registered figures out of the pre-registration and compares them to the frozen analysis module, so the document and the code cannot drift apart without the build failing. There are still no results. The conditions under which the hypothesis is considered refuted remain fixed, and a null result will be published.

title: An Agent Framework for Real-Time Financial Information Searching with Large Language Models
abstract: Financial decision-making requires processing vast amounts of real-time information while understanding their complex temporal relationships. While traditional search engines excel at providing real-time information access, they often struggle to comprehend sophisticated user intentions and contextual nuances. Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate reasoning and interaction capabilities but may generate unreliable outputs without access to current data. While recent attempts have been made to combine LLMs with search capabilities, they suffer from (1) restricted access to specialized financial data, (2) static query structures that cannot adapt to dynamic market conditions, and (3) insufficient temporal awareness in result generation. To address these challenges, we present FinSearch, a novel agent-based search framework specifically designed for financial applications that interface with diverse financial data sources including market, stock, and news data. Innovatively, FinSearch comprises four components: (1) an LLM-based multi-step search pre-planner that decomposes user queries into structured sub-queries mapped to specific data sources through a graph representation; (2) a search executor with an LLM-based adaptive query rewriter that executes the searching of each sub-query while dynamically refining the sub-queries in its subsequent node based on intermediate search results; (3) a temporal weighting mechanism that prioritizes information relevance based on the deduced time context from the user's query; (4) an LLM-based response generator that synthesizes results into coherent, contextually appropriate outputs. To evaluate FinSearch, we construct FinSearchBench-24, a benchmark of 1,500 four-choice questions across the stock market, rate changes, monetary policy, and industry developments spanning from June to October 2024.

title: Energy-Efficient Deep Reinforcement Learning with Spiking Transformers
abstract: Agent-based Transformers have been widely adopted in recent reinforcement learning advances due to their demonstrated ability to solve complex tasks. However, the high computational complexity of Transformers often results in significant energy consumption, limiting their deployment in real-world autonomous systems. Spiking neural networks (SNNs), with their biologically inspired structure, offer an energy-efficient alternative for machine learning. In this paper, a novel Spike-Transformer Reinforcement Learning (STRL) algorithm that combines the energy efficiency of SNNs with the powerful decision-making capabilities of reinforcement learning is developed. Specifically, an SNN using multi-step Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons and attention mechanisms capable of processing spatio-temporal patterns over multiple time steps is designed. The architecture is further enhanced with state, action, and reward encodings to create a Transformer-like structure optimized for reinforcement learning tasks. Comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on state-of-the-art benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed SNN Transformer achieves significantly improved policy performance compared to conventional agent-based Transformers. With both enhanced energy efficiency and policy optimality, this work highlights a promising direction for deploying bio-inspired, low-cost machine learning models in complex real-world decision-making scenarios.

title: Scaling Strategies of SIMCAST for Late Blight: Training and Modernizing Decision Support for Wider Adoption
abstract: This report documents the scaling pathway of SIMCAST, a decision support system (DSS) for potato late blight (Phytophthora infestans), designed to translate weather-driven disease-risk modeling into actionable fungicide-timing recommendations that reduce avoidable yield losses and unnecessary pesticide use. Implemented with partners across Peru, Ecuador, and India, the initiative combined capacity building and user feedback with major technical modernization: the Lateblight Advisor web app was upgraded from an initial R/Shiny prototype to Shiny for Python, enabling stronger integration with modern data and AI workflows and real-time weather inputs (WeatherAPI); a SIMCAST Model Context Protocol (MCP) was developed to expose standardized model tools for multi-channel deployment; and GeoSIMCAST extended point-based modeling to national-scale risk mapping using gridded climate products and reconstructed dew point temperature (Tdew) to support humidity-driven risk estimation. Evidence from 30 farmer demonstration trials (2025) with resistant cultivars (Pollera and Watia) indicates that SIMCAST-guided scheduling can reduce disease intensity and optimize spray frequency, while yield responses warrant continued evaluation under broader field conditions. Together, these advances position SIMCAST as an interoperable, scalable digital advisory service that supports smarter fungicide use—right product, right timing, only when needed—and provide a clear strategy for wider adoption through phased scaling, partnerships, and extension-oriented delivery.
venue: CGSPace A Repository of Agricultural Research Outputs (Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research)

title: TOWARDS ROBUST AND SAFE AI-ENABLED AUTONOMOUS SYSTEMS THROUGH DIAGNOSTICS AND DEBUGGING
abstract: Autonomous systems are shifting from handcrafted, rule-based architectures to deeply integrated, AI-enabled ecosystems in which perception, adaptation, and reasoning are tightly interwoven with classical planning. While this evolution has expanded capability, it has also complicated trust: the interdependence of learned components make diagnosis, debugging, and assurance substantially harder. This thesis develops a diagnostics- and debugging-centered framework for improving robustness and safety across the core layers of autonomy.At the planning layer, I introduce a root-cause analysis framework ROCAS for rule-based decision pipelines in autonomous systems. The framework traces observed anomalous behaviors back to misconfigurations, providing causal attributions. By turning behavior-level observations into configuration-level evidence, it strengthens explainability and supports systematic safety auditing.At the adaptation layer, I develop a diagnostics-driven framework EffiTune that mitigates training inefficiency in parameter-tuning models for autonomous systems. EffiTune ﬁrst performs behavior-guided diagnostics to locate bottlenecks and underrepresented, failure-critical regions in the environment; it then applies targeted up-sampling to rebalance the training distribution, eliminating redundant sampling and mitigating training inefficiency.At the perception layer, I develop techniques DECREE to detect hidden backdoors in foundation vision encoders that provide features to downstream tasks. These methods expose subtle data-poisoning and model-manipulation behaviors and act as early-stage defenses, preserving the integrity of perceptual inputs on which planning and adaptation depend.Finally, at the reasoning layer, I propose an intent testing framework TAI3 for large language model (LLM) agents that orchestrate tools for task completion. The framework systematically exposes and characterizes failure modes in which agents misuse tools or deviate from user intent, yielding fine-grained diagnostics of reasoning reliability and intent integrity in LLM agent systems. Collectively, these contributions form a cohesive, multi-layered approach to enhancing reliability, interpretability, and safety in autonomous systems. By bridging classical planning with data-driven adaptation, safeguarding perception, and auditing agentic reasoning, the thesis advances practical methods for diagnosis and debugging, laying the groundwork for more trustworthy autonomous intelligence.

title: Symbolic Constraint Agents: Mining Formal Tool-Call Constraints to Prevent Agent Errors
abstract: Symbolic constraints (programmatic, deterministic checks for tool calls) enable deterministic verification of LLM agents' tool calls, but existing approaches primarily enforce predefined safety policies rather than tool dependencies in complex tool environments. We explore whether symbolic constraints can be mined from environments and observations beyond predefined policies, and whether they can improve end-to-end task performance. We present Symbolic Constraint Agents (SCA), a framework that mines symbolic constraints from API documentation, refines them against execution traces, and checks the agent's tool calls with an SMT solver at runtime. A violation triggers a natural-language warning or, when the valid replacement is uniquely determined, an automatic repair. On AppWorld, refinement raises error-detection F1 from 37.0 to 58.3 on GPT-5.5 traces and from 39.3 to 61.9 on Qwen3.5-27B traces. At runtime, repair raises GPT-5.4-mini's task success by 5.4 points under a 40-call budget and 9.8 points when environment errors are hidden, while removing 59--87\% of failed calls across models, and transfers to $τ^2$-bench with gains of up to 5.6 points. These findings show that automatically acquired symbolic constraints can improve tool-calling reliability and task completion, particularly when failures are costly or difficult to diagnose.

title: When the Agent Is the Adversary: Architectural Requirements for Agentic AI Containment After the April 2026 Frontier Model Escape
abstract: The April 2026 disclosure that a frontier large language model escaped its security sandbox, executed unauthorized actions, and concealed its modifications to version control history demonstrates that agentic AI systems with autonomous tool access can circumvent the containment mechanisms designed to constrain them. This paper analyzes four categories of current containment approaches - alignment training, environmental sandboxing, application-level tool-call interception, and accessible audit systems - and identifies the failure modes each exhibits when the AI agent is treated as a potential adversary rather than a trusted component receiving adversarial inputs. We categorize five behavioral incidents from the public disclosure and situate them within 698 real-world AI scheming incidents documented by the Centre for Long-Term Resilience between October 2025 and March 2026, a 4.9x acceleration establishing the challenge as systemic. We derive five architectural requirements: trust separation through layered OS privilege enforcement with semantic intent analysis, sequential intent inference through five-phase taxonomic monitoring, independent containment integrity monitoring, adversarial audit isolation through logical invisibility, and emergent capability envelope enforcement through distributional divergence monitoring. No publicly described system satisfies all five. We argue that architectural containment is the only durable safety strategy given the inevitable proliferation of equivalent capabilities including open-weight models. The author's published patent portfolio in provider-independent constraint enforcement addresses several of these requirements. Concurrent work including SandboxEscapeBench (arXiv:2603.02277) independently confirms that frontier models can escape standard container sandboxes, corroborating the threat model presented here.

title: Inequality Challenged and Restored
abstract: In the 1710s, under pressure from an ongoing war, Sweden’s absolute king, Charles XII, implemented a number of fiscal and monetary measures that displayed a disdain for traditional privileges and carried a potential for social change. Taxation was made progressive and credit became more important to finance the war. Liquidity was radically expanded, most significantly by the release of very large amounts of fiat coins. Following the death of Charles XII in November 1718, there was a political reaction against the war policies and the fiscal and monetary measures were reversed, resulting in the dismantling of royal absolutism and a partial government default. This study consists of two parts. In the first, we investigate the impact of the war policy and the monetary measures of Charles XII’s regime on the social redistribution of resources in Swedish society, especially in the years 1715 to 1718. In the second, we focus on how the socioeconomic changes were addressed by political agents between the death of Charles XII and the default of 1719. Our results show that the fiat money permeated the economy and reached all social groups, and that in some locations its distribution upset the prevailing social order. Peasants and other low-ranking groups were targeted by the partial default, which largely deprived them of their monetary assets.

title: Learning-Based Collaborative Control for Bi-Manual Tactile-Reactive Grasping
abstract: Grasping is a core task in robotics with various applications. However, most current implementations are primarily designed for rigid items, and their performance drops considerably when handling fragile or deformable materials that require real-time feedback. Meanwhile, tactile-reactive grasping focuses on a single agent, which limits their ability to grasp and manipulate large, heavy objects. To overcome this, we propose a learning-based, tactile-reactive multi-agent Model Predictive Controller (MPC) for grasping a wide range of objects with different softness and shapes, beyond the capabilities of preexisting single-agent implementations. Our system uses two Gelsight Mini tactile sensors [1] to extract real-time information on object texture and stiffness. This rich tactile feedback is used to estimate contact dynamics and object compliance in real time, enabling the system to adapt its control policy to diverse object geometries and stiffness profiles. The learned controller operates in a closed loop, leveraging tactile encoding to predict grasp stability and adjust force and position accordingly. Our key technical contributions include a multi-agent MPC formulation trained on real contact interactions, a tactile-data driven method for inferring grasping states, and a coordination strategy that enables collaborative control. By combining tactile sensing and a learning-based multi-agent MPC, our method offers a robust, intelligent solution for collaborative grasping in complex environments, significantly advancing the capabilities of multi-agent systems. Our approach is validated through extensive experiments against independent PD and MPC baselines. Our pipeline outperforms the baselines regarding success rates in achieving and maintaining stable grasps across objects of varying sizes and stiffness.

title: Agent Security Meets Regulatory Reality -- A Practitioner Systematization of Autonomous-Agent Threats and Controls in Regulated Financial Systems
abstract: Large language model agents are entering regulated financial systems, yet the security literature characterizing their attack surface is almost entirely laboratory-based, and the practitioner guidance on regulated deployment is neither peer-reviewed nor connected to a formal threat model. We bridge the two from production experience. We map six established agentic threat categories namely prompt injection, identity and authorization, action auditability, tool abuse, data residency, and boundary policy enforcement onto the specific control obligations imposed by the US and the EU financial regulation (ECOA and Regulation B, the EU AI Act, GDPR Article 22, and FINRA's 2026 agent guidance), showing how legal accountability amplifies each threat relative to an unregulated deployment. We then document four architectural patterns from a production Know Your Customer deployment for a consumer credit product (A2A compliance choreography, grounded-RAG-for-audit, case-ID propagation, and an inference-boundary redaction proxy) that moved a multi-day manual process to same-day automated resolution for roughly four in five cases. Finally, we report three negative results, including two control failures surfaced only by internal audit and a population of legitimate applicants the automated pipeline cannot serve. Securing agents under regulation, we conclude, is less about novel attack classes than about making auditability, least-privilege authorization, and boundary policy enforcement real at production scale -- requirements current agent frameworks leave to the deploying engineer.

title: From pathogenesis to antigens: the key to shaping the future of TB vaccines
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the gravest global health challenges. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis), the causative agent, employs sophisticated immune evasion and pathogenesis strategies. Its capability to thrive within immune cells and incite robust inflammatory responses prolongs infection and dissemination. Mycobacterial advanced adaptations facilitate navigation through the human immune system and present a variable antigenic profile throughout different infection stages. Investigating these strategies unfolds targeted approaches to effective vaccine development against TB. This review delves into the most advanced and exhaustive insights into the immune evasion tactics and pathogenic processes of M. tuberculosis across various infection stages. The knowledge distilled from this analysis holds the promise of guiding the creation of innovative TB vaccines and translating theoretical groundwork into practical immunological defenses.

title: Learning from Teacher Continuations at Student States
abstract: We present OLIVE (OnLine InterVEntion). At each iteration, the evolving student policy generates a new prefix, the teacher continues it autoregressively, and the student is updated using cross-entropy computed on the teacher-generated tokens. Each design choice targets a corresponding limitation of existing distillation methods: (1) sequential covariate shift in offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on fixed teacher trajectories, (2) fragmented supervision under prefix failure in token-level on-policy distillation (OPD), and (3) the need for access to teacher token probabilities in distribution-matching distillation. OLIVE achieves higher reasoning performance than OPD (with a top-16 KL approximation) at comparable GPU-hour cost. Our asynchronous implementation further reduces OLIVE's total training time by 23.8\%. We evaluate OLIVE on both hard reasoning tasks and agentic tasks which reflects modern post-training scenarios, and it consistently outperforms existing distillation methods under the same training budget. By regenerating prefixes from the evolving student, OLIVE continues improving after offline distillation plateaus while better preserving the general capabilities and plasticity of the student. Using only text from GPT-5.4-mini, continuously training with OLIVE outperforms offline SFT from the same teacher by 13\% on ScienceWorld. These results support OLIVE as an effective and efficient approach to online language-model distillation.

title: Strategic reinforcement learning agents for autonomous cyber defense
abstract: Ubiquitous computing is now a reality for organizations worldwide, and the security of these systems is of paramount importance for operations across industry, academia, and government. However, the deluge of information given to security operations teams is challenging to respond to at scale and has led to significant interest in automation and autonomous cyber operations -- the automated investigation and remediation of cybersecurity incidents. Despite widespread adoption of machine learning and artificial intelligence in the cybersecurity domain, reinforcement learning has, to date, not been widely leveraged in autonomous cyber operations despite its seemingly natural fit. In this work, we identify four "fatal flaws'' in autonomous cyber operations research: state space observability, attacker knowledge of the environment, defender knowledge of the attacker, and the assumption of a fixed-size state space. Via game theory, decision theory, and experimentation with reinforcement learning agents, we address each of these limitations to bridge the gap between the current state of the art in research and what has been adopted in practice. In particular, we explore the theoretical value of partial observability and find that this result has significant practical effect in designing both attacking and defending agents. Using reinforcement learning, we demonstrate that there is a "price of pessimism'' for overestimating an attacker's capability. By modifying the YAWNING-TITAN and CybORG environments, we explore the impact of training agents on attackers with different objectives and consider the impact of using standard proximal policy optimization versus hierarchical proximal policy optimization, finding that there are trade-offs between the two. Finally, we introduce an agent architecture that incorporates a transformer for representation learning that allows our agents to operate in dynamic state spaces. Through these contributions, we bridge the gap between the current academic state of the art and the needs of cybersecurity practitioners, enabling important future work on autonomous cyber operations.

title: Graph of Trace: Visualizing Execution Traces of Scientific Agent
abstract: Scientific AI agents can autonomously carry out complex research workflows, yet these unfolded workflows often remain difficult for humans to inspect and review, limiting interpretable, controllable and effective human-AI collaboration. To address this challenge, we present a monitoring and visualization framework that records fine-grained execution events and organizes them into a directed graph that makes agent workflows explicit as they proceed. The system records intermediate steps (e.g. tool calls and code executions), and renders them as real-time updated visual traces that expose workflow structure. This allows users to examine how results are produced, identify where failures emerge, and better understand agent behavior across different stages of the research process. We conduct an evaluation on complex research tasks with domain experts of interdisciplinary backgrounds in AI, neuroscience, and biology. Experts report that structured traces visualization improves understanding of agent workflows, perceived interpretability, and usability for analysis and further interaction.

title: A Policy-Based Blackboard Control Mechanism for Dynamic Prioritization in Multilayered Problems
abstract: This research introduces a new blackboard control mechanism designed to address the weaknesses of conventional systems in managing complex, multilayered problem domains. Existing approaches are constrained by rigid, sequential control structures and limited scalability, making them unsuitable for environments that require adaptive and flexible decision-making. The proposed mechanism provides a standardized coordination framework capable of prioritizing several primary problems along with their associated subproblems. As a proof of concept, the control mechanism is applied to the domain of sustainable timber harvesting, a field characterized by interdependent tasks such as inventory assessment, growth prediction, ecological impact mitigation, and strategic tree selection. The mechanism supports dynamic problem prioritization according to a policy-based technique, allowing the system to adapt to progressing problem-solving needs. This study demonstrates the potential of an improved blackboard control mechanism to enhance decision support in complex, real-world domains.

title: Editorial: Generative AI and large language models in medicine: applications, challenges, and opportunities
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has entered medicine through a heterogeneous set of uses rather than through a single technological pathway. Large language models now draft clinical text, interpret reports, answer patient questions, support knowledge retrieval, structure health data, assist education, and participate in increasingly complex decision support workflows. The 34 contributions assembled in this Research Topic capture that breadth across clinical medicine, public health, digital health, oncology, rehabilitation, mental health, nursing, health informatics, education, quality management, and biomedical policy. Their collective value lies less in any single performance estimate than in the opportunity to examine what changes when language model research moves from demonstrations of linguistic competence toward systems that must operate under clinical constraints.The studies concerned with diagnosis, staging, and clinical reasoning show why this distinction matters. In a two institution study of 552 PET CT reports across six cancers, Xu et al. found that GPT 5 achieved 82.1 percent overall TNM staging accuracy compared with 77.0 percent for junior radiologists, while repeated model agreement was close to perfect. Performance nevertheless differed across cancer types and was weakest for metastatic staging. Dinç et al. reported an analogous pattern in radiation oncology. GPT 5 reached 92.8 percent on a standardized examination benchmark, substantially exceeding earlier GPT generations, yet authentic clinical vignettes still produced substantive errors in cases requiring precise trial knowledge or detailed adaptation to clinical context. The high benchmark score therefore did not remove the need for specialist review.Other studies reinforce the task dependent character of performance. Pan et al. found that DeepSeek V3.1, ChatGPT 5, and Grok 4 answered more than 90 percent of guideline derived bone cancer questions correctly in both evaluation rounds, although model specific strengths remained. In maternal venous thromboembolism care, Li et al. found superior overall expert ratings for GPT 4.1, Claude 3.7, and DeepSeek across education, care planning, and prevention, but explicitly did not interpret those results as evidence of readiness for independent nursing deployment. Konzmann et al., synthesizing 31 tumor board studies and 3,845 cases, identified a broader complexity gap: concordance was strongest in standardized and common oncological settings and deteriorated in rare, multimodal, or clinically ambiguous cases.This evidence is compatible with the conceptual position advanced by Greengrass, who treats AI as a potential support for human clinical reasoning rather than as a replacement for it. Human reasoning is constrained by working memory, cognitive load, fatigue, anchoring, and other biases, whereas computational systems can search and compare information at scales that exceed unaided cognition. The collection, however, does not support the inference that computational scale removes clinical uncertainty. Its more defensible implication is a risk gradient. Language models appear most reliable when the task has explicit rules, sufficiently complete textual evidence, and an auditable reference standard. Their reliability becomes more difficult to establish as the task requires multimodal interpretation, rare disease knowledge, rapidly changing evidence, patient specific tradeoffs, or judgments for which several clinically defensible answers may exist.A second theme concerns the architecture surrounding the language model. Several contributions suggest that the clinically relevant object is increasingly the full system rather than the foundation model in isolation. Barlow et al. fine-tuned an open Llama model to identify actionable incidental findings in PET CT reports and achieved a document level F1 score of 0.917 internally and 0.79 on an external test set. The reduction under external evaluation is itself informative, because differences in reporting style and institutional practice remain consequential even when internal performance is strong.Grounding methods address a different source of error. Kokash et al. combined ontology-based retrieval with LLM semantic adjudication for healthcare data harmonization and reported expert agreement as high as 92 percent. Retrieval alone was insufficient; the gain came from pairing broad candidate retrieval with model based semantic validation. Chen et al. provide a related demonstration through a knowledge graph system for Jin San Zhen therapy. Their hybrid architecture outperformed the general model on correctness, professionalism, and completeness, while the knowledge enhanced outputs remained traceable to source literature and no fabricated claims were detected in the evaluated question set. Sugihara et al. extend this architectural reasoning to the choice between open and proprietary models. Proprietary systems may offer stronger schema adherence or complex reasoning in some tasks, whereas open models provide advantages in local control, auditability, customization, privacy, and cost. The practical choice therefore depends on the clinical task and governance environment rather than on a universal model ranking.Bounded documentation and evidence processing tasks may be among the more defensible near term applications, but they still require verification. Aiumtrakul et al. found strong clinical reasoning in 89.7 percent of ChatGPT 5 generated nephrology prior authorization letters, yet diagnostic coding was correct in 79.3 percent and citation errors remained. Oami et al. observed high performance for background data extraction in systematic reviews, but outcome extraction was markedly more variable and repeated session consistency declined for the harder task. More elaborate prompting produced only modest accuracy changes while increasing processing time. Khoruzhaya et al. place these findings in methodological context: their review of medical text summarization reported external validation in only 7 percent of studies and patient safety assessment in only 3 percent, with wide variation in reported hallucination rates. Their MEDAI LLM SUMM checklist accordingly emphasizes clinical validity, prompt documentation, expert evaluation, hallucination assessment, safety, and data availability. Zhu et al., using eight models to generate medical examination questions and answers from real world EHRs, further show that models can approach clinicians on selected dimensions while human authors retain advantages in information sufficiency and overall answer quality.Taken together, these studies distinguish prompt engineering from clinical system engineering. Prompt design can improve instructions, but evidence grounding, model adaptation, structured outputs, local deployment, source traceability, safety rules, and expert adjudication determine whether an apparently competent model can be integrated into a reproducible workflow.Patient facing applications expose another limitation of accuracy centered evaluation. Graca et al. found that healthcare professionals rated ChatGPT responses more favourably than established evidence based PCOS responses for 11 of 12 questions, and further simplification improved readability. Yet the wider collection shows that medical correctness does not guarantee communicative usefulness. Joseph et al. found that cardiovascular responses changed in complexity with the education level implied by the prompt, but output frequently remained above ordinary health literacy needs. Wang et al. on gestational diabetes reported 92.17 percent mean accuracy for ChatGPT 5 on standardized questions and favourable reliability ratings, while all evaluated models still exceeded the recommended sixth grade reading level and showed poor transparency under JAMA criteria. Huang et al. reached a similar result for perinatal depression: responses were often informative and empathetic, but readability remained excessive and clinical safety behaviours were incomplete.The chronic heart failure study by Wang et al. on chronic heart failure adds actionability to this evaluation framework. Overall content quality was favourable, but median actionability was only 20 percent, and the most complete output was also among the least readable. This reveals a structural tradeoff that cannot be captured by accuracy alone. Albaz et al. likewise found favourable clarity and tone in ChatGPT 5 responses about vasectomy, but medical accuracy and completeness varied across questions and expert agreement was very low. Patient validation was absent. Angyal et al. approach the same problem from the user side by developing a questionnaire to measure how adults use ChatGPT for primary and secondary disease prevention, providing a basis for studying behaviour rather than assuming that availability translates into appropriate use.Two contributions show how patient and caregiver support may be made more constrained. Hanzawa et al. combined a domain specific knowledge base, retrieval augmented generation, sentiment analysis, explicit safety restrictions, and escalation rules in an agent supporting families implementing treatment for adolescent anorexia nervosa. Experts rated 91.6 percent of 477 responses as clinically appropriate, but the authors appropriately call for usability testing and randomized evaluation of caregiver burden, adherence, and clinical outcomes. O'Malley et al. similarly describe retrieval, system instructions, and fine tuning as complementary strategies for customized physical activity chatbots, while emphasizing human evaluation, privacy, and operational cost.These studies support a multidimensional definition of patient facing quality. Accuracy and completeness remain necessary, but safe communication also requires readability, actionability, source traceability, uncertainty communication, cultural and educational fit, and evidence that users understand what the system has told them.Clinical implementation depends on professionals as well as models. Among Italian physiotherapists, Deodato et al. found widespread awareness of AI chatbots but limited clinical use: 66.9 percent had never used them in practice even though 78 percent expressed a positive attitude toward future adoption. Concerns centred on patient self diagnosis, false information, and loss of human interaction. In a sample drawn principally from Ecuador, Cherrez Ojeda et al. similarly found cautious optimism, but only 31.99 percent had used ChatGPT and 67.85 percent of familiar respondents regarded sole source clinical use as unethical. Safi et al. documented a different mismatch in surgical education: 80.9 percent had prior ChatGPT experience, yet 93.2 percent lacked formal AI training. Informal exposure is therefore advancing faster than structured professional education.The multimodal papers widen the definition of clinical AI while also illustrating why adding data modalities should not be assumed to improve performance. Manir et al. combined textual embeddings with acoustic summaries for affective tone analysis in aphasia. Under recording separated evaluation, the fused model did not outperform the text only model, and human agreement on aphasic affect was low. Hussain et al. review evidence in depression detection showing benefits from combining EEG, speech, facial, and linguistic signals, but also report the familiar decline from controlled laboratory results to more ecologically representative datasets. Siefert et al. demonstrate that smaller fine tuned models can approximate expert psychological ratings of complex narratives, particularly when model outputs are ensembled, yet they retain human supervision as the appropriate clinical frame.Multimodality also creates new risks. Jędrasiak and Bijoch examine synthetic audiovisual material in telemedicine and teledentistry, showing that manipulation can threaten diagnostic evidence, communication, and medico legal documentation. Their work makes provenance part of clinical safety. Trustworthy generative AI cannot be defined only by whether generated text is factually correct; healthcare systems must also be able to establish whether the data supplied to an AI system, or returned through a digital encounter, are authentic.The collection therefore shifts attention from model capability toward an evaluation and governance problem. Knott et al. show that healthcare AI studies still concentrate disproportionately on accuracy while paying far less attention to fairness, calibration, deployment readiness, and actual patient care. Their European analysis also makes clear that regulatory obligations depend on intended function and clinical risk. Administrative quality tools and systems that influence diagnosis or treatment cannot be governed as equivalent applications. Wang, Hao and Chen extend the accountability question into pharmaceutical intellectual property, where AI assisted discovery raises unresolved issues concerning inventorship, copyright, and ownership across jurisdictions.Reproducibility deserves particular attention. A clinical system that changes a medically material recommendation when the patient information has not changed poses a different problem from a deterministic medical device, even if its average performance is favourable. The tumor board literature synthesized by Konzmann et al. reports substantial variation in repeated response consistency and incomplete reporting of model inference settings across studies. Oami et al. likewise show that repeated session consistency can deteriorate as extraction becomes more complex. Model updates introduce another layer of temporal instability because the product evaluated today may not be behaviourally identical to the product deployed later.The evidence across the Research Topic supports a risk proportionate interpretation of human oversight. Lower consequence, reversible, and auditable tasks such as drafting, extraction, summarization, and guideline retrieval are plausible candidates for supervised implementation. Patient communication and guideline based decision support require stronger controls because deficiencies in readability, actionability, or omitted context may affect behaviour. Diagnosis, staging, treatment recommendation, and other high consequence applications require prospective validation, explicit uncertainty handling, and clinician accountability. Human review should therefore be designed into the workflow rather than appended as a generic disclaimer.Figure 1 represents this translational logic. Foundation model capability is only the first stage. Task adaptation must be followed by evidence grounding, workflow integration, clinical validation, and continuous governance. Human oversight, external validation, reproducibility, evidence traceability, health literacy and equity, privacy, and accountability operate across the pathway rather than at a single endpoint. This structure also explains why no universally superior medical language model emerges from the collection. Different systems lead on different endpoints, and the preferred model changes with the task, population, infrastructure, privacy requirements, and tolerance for error. The 34 contributions document a field moving from proof of language competence toward the science of accountable clinical integration. Contemporary models can perform useful work in structured clinical reasoning, data extraction, patient education, documentation, knowledge retrieval, psychological assessment, and administrative processes. They can sometimes match or exceed junior clinicians or established information sources on narrowly defined measures. Those findings are scientifically relevant, but they are not equivalent to evidence of autonomous clinical readiness.The next phase of research should therefore privilege prospective and multicentre evaluation, external validation across institutions and populations, repeated testing for response stability, explicit reporting of model versions and inference conditions, patient centred endpoints, economic evaluation, fairness assessment, and post deployment surveillance. Grounded architectures using curated retrieval, ontologies, knowledge graphs, local models, and explicit escalation rules warrant continued evaluation because they make model behaviour more constrained and auditable. Clinical AI literacy must develop in parallel so that professionals can judge uncertainty, verify sources, protect patient data, recognize inappropriate automation, and retain responsibility for consequential decisions.Generative AI is becoming useful in medicine before it has become uniformly trustworthy. The evidence in this Research Topic suggests that the appropriate response is neither unrestricted adoption nor categorical rejection. The defensible path is selective integration in which technical capability is matched to clinical risk, evidence is made traceable, validation extends beyond benchmark accuracy, and accountability remains explicit throughout the system lifecycle.
